questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What address translation conceals and what it leaves visible
questions.learningObjective: Identify what address translation conceals and what it leaves visible.
questions.stem: Ticket OPS-118 asks why a workstation behind the office gateway appears to the outside internet as a single public address.

options.text: The gateway replaces the source address with one from its public pool and reverses it on reply
The gateway encrypts every outbound payload so the internal address never appears on the wire
options.misconception: believes hiding the internal address requires payload encryption

options.text: Each workstation hides behind a separate proxy process installed on the host by the administrator
options.misconception: assumes each host runs its own proxy rather than one gateway

options.text: The original address survives the trip and the public address is added as an extra header field
options.misconception: believes a second address is added and the original kept

questions.explanation: Address translation rewrites the source address to one shared public address and restores the mapping on reply. Encrypting the payload would hide content but does not conceal the internal address.
questions.hint: Think about which field the gateway rewrites.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What an untrusted route announcement permits
questions.learningObjective: Determine which traffic an untrusted route announcement can divert.
questions.stem: Ticket NET-204 records a prefix announcement accepted from a peer that the team never authorised and asks which traffic can now be diverted.

options.text: Only traffic to the exact addresses listed in the announcement prefix will be diverted
options.misconception: assumes only listed host addresses are affected by the prefix

options.text: Traffic addressed to the announced prefix can be sent along the announced path by whoever sent it
The announcement lets the peer decrypt traffic that was already encrypted before it left
options.misconception: believes a route announcement grants decryption of live traffic

options.text: The announcement grants the peer administrative rights on every router inside the region
options.misconception: confuses route control with authority over the devices

questions.explanation: An accepted announcement redirects traffic for the whole announced prefix, so its originator can steer that traffic. It carries no keys and no device rights, and never narrows to single host addresses.
questions.hint: Think about the unit of routing: prefixes, not hosts.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What a domain-key signature deliberately excludes
questions.learningObjective: Describe what a domain-key signature deliberately leaves out of the trust it establishes.
questions.stem: Ticket MAIL-31 asks the team to describe what the signature added to a message never covers, so support staff stop promising end-to-end secrecy.

answer.exemplar: The signature proves the message body originated with the holder of the domain signing key and was not altered in transit. It deliberately says nothing about the content itself, the recipients, whether the key holder was authorised to write, or whether anyone on the path read the message.

questions.explanation: The signature binds content to a signing key but offers no confidentiality and no statement about the human author. It does not encrypt the body or report who read the message.
questions.hint: Ask what the signature proves, then what it leaves out.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What the alignment rule in a reporting record adds
questions.learningObjective: Explain what the alignment rule adds to a message authenticity decision.

stimulus.body: A policy record for the sending domain asks that every message from it satisfy the policy record and pass a relaxed match between the visible sender name and the visible domain. The ticket asks the reviewer to explain what that second requirement adds.

questions.stem: In ticket POL-9, what does the alignment requirement add to the decision that a message is genuine?

options.text: It requires the message body to be signed with the private key of the receiving organisation
options.misconception: believes alignment means the receiver signs inbound mail

options.text: It requires the sending host to publish a fresh policy record for every individual message
options.misconception: assumes alignment forces per-message policy publication

options.text: It requires the visible sender identity to be consistent with the domain that passed the policy check
It requires the message to be forwarded through the domain's own outbound relays only
options.misconception: thinks alignment forces routing through the sender relays

questions.explanation: Alignment ties the visible sender name to the domain whose policy record passed, so a forged visible name still fails. It demands no new keys and does not constrain the relays used.
questions.hint: Alignment compares two names that the ticket already shows.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: Why forwarding breaks sender authorisation
questions.learningObjective: Explain why forwarding breaks the authorisation a receiver can rely on.
questions.stem: Ticket MAIL-52 asks about a colleague who forwards an external message to the internal list and asks which two facts explain the outcome.

options.text: The signature covers the original message, and forwarding does not change the author of the delivered copy
options.misconception: believes a forwarded copy keeps the original author

options.text: Forwarding strips the signature entirely, and the list therefore receives an unverified message
options.misconception: assumes forwarding always removes the signature from the copy

options.text: The signature covers the original message, and forwarding renews the signature using the colleague key
options.misconception: thinks forwarding re-signs the copy with the forwarder key

options.text: The signature covers the original message, and forwarding creates a new message whose author is now the colleague

questions.explanation: The signature covers the bytes it was made over, so it verifies on the original message. The copy reaching the list is a new message from the forwarder, so the original authorisation no longer applies.
questions.hint: Split it into what is proved and what is omitted.

questions.topic: What the chain of trust in signed name resolution establishes
questions.learningObjective: Explain what the chain of trust in signed name resolution establishes.
questions.stem: Ticket DNS-14 asks what the signed delegation from the root down to a company zone actually proves when a lookup succeeds.

options.text: The name is registered to the company that published the zone and to nobody else
options.misconception: confuses a signed delegation proof with a legal ownership claim

options.text: The answer was signed by a key that chains to a trust anchor the resolver already trusts
The answer is the most recent one published and no other publisher was involved
options.misconception: assumes signing proves the answer was the most recent

options.text: The company that owns the zone has paid an authority to vouch for its records
options.misconception: believes a signature is proof that a fee was paid to a registry

questions.explanation: The chain shows that the answering zone holds a key descending from an anchor the resolver already accepts. It says nothing about legal ownership, payment, or which publisher was most recent.
questions.hint: Follow the key hierarchy, not the invoice trail.

questions.topic: The registration step signed resolution does not cover
questions.learningObjective: Identify the registration step that signed resolution does not cover.
questions.stem: Ticket DNS-22 separates registration from resolution and asks which stage is left outside the signed chain of trust.

options.text: Registering a domain name with a registrar, which is handled outside the delegation chain
Resolving a name to a set of addresses using the signed records published for the zone
options.misconception: believes the signed chain covers the lookup that returns addresses

options.text: Caching a signed answer at the resolver so that later lookups avoid the hierarchy
options.misconception: assumes caching is the stage the signature does not cover

options.text: Publishing the signed delegation record that links a parent zone to a child zone
options.misconception: thinks the delegation record is the unsigned part of the chain

questions.explanation: The signed chain covers delegation and the zone records used to answer a query. The act of registering a name with a registrar happens outside that chain and carries no signature a resolver can check.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What an untrusted route announcement permits
questions.learningObjective: Explain the consequence of accepting an unauthorised route announcement.
questions.stem: Ticket NET-19 asks for a written explanation of what happens when a prefix announcement from an unauthorised source is accepted by a router.

answer.exemplar: Accepting the announcement makes the router send traffic for that prefix toward the announcing source, so the source can receive, delay, or drop it and can also deliver it to a host it controls. Nothing about the announcement is authenticated unless a separate cryptographic check is configured and validated before trust is granted.

questions.explanation: An accepted announcement changes where traffic for a prefix is sent, giving its originator a vantage point over it. The route carries no proof of identity, so the router believes it because sending was permitted.
questions.hint: Separate control over routing from proof of the sender.

questions.topic: What a sender policy record states and who evaluates it
questions.learningObjective: Identify which organisation evaluates a sender policy record.

stimulus.body: A drawing in ticket MSG-60 shows one sending domain, one published policy record, and two separate checks performed by the receiving organisation rather than by the sender. The ticket asks which organisation decides whether a message passes.

questions.stem: In the flow shown in ticket MSG-60, which organisation evaluates the sender policy record against an arriving message?

options.text: The receiving organisation, because the policy record is published for others to check
The sending organisation, because it wrote the policy and therefore applies it
options.misconception: believes the publisher of a policy also performs the check

options.text: The registrar that holds the domain registration, because it controls the domain
options.misconception: thinks registration transfers checking to the registrar

options.text: The internet registry that publishes policy records for every top-level domain
options.misconception: assumes a central registry checks every domain policy

questions.explanation: A sender policy record is published so that receivers can test arriving mail against it. The sender does not evaluate its own arriving traffic, and no registry or registrar performs the check for the recipient.
questions.hint: Ask who benefits from running the check.

questions.stem: Ticket MAIL-42 needs a two-part answer: first name what the signature establishes, then name what it deliberately leaves unsaid.

options.text: It establishes that signed content came from the key holder, and it leaves out only the sending time
options.misconception: believes the only thing excluded is the sending time

options.text: It establishes that the message reached the intended recipient, and it leaves out confidentiality
options.misconception: thinks the signature proves delivery to the recipient

options.text: It establishes that the recipient holds the matching key, and it leaves out the identity of the author
options.misconception: confuses who holds the signing key with who the recipient is

options.text: It establishes that signed content came from the key holder, and it leaves out confidentiality and authorship

questions.explanation: The signature ties the signed bytes to a key, so it establishes origin in the key sense only. It says nothing about confidentiality, delivery, or the human author.
questions.hint: Split it into what is proved and what is omitted.

questions.topic: What the alignment rule in a reporting record adds
questions.learningObjective: Explain why an alignment rule supplements a policy check.
questions.stem: Ticket POL-12 asks why a policy record needs an alignment rule in addition to the policy check itself.

options.text: Because a policy check alone cannot confirm that the domain published the policy record
options.misconception: believes a policy check cannot confirm the publisher

options.text: Because a policy check alone leaves the message body readable to anyone on the network path
options.misconception: thinks the policy check leaves the body exposed in transit

options.text: Because a policy check alone accepts a message whose visible sender identity was forged
Because a policy check alone cannot tell whether the host was compromised
options.misconception: believes the policy check detects a compromised host

questions.explanation: A policy check tests sending infrastructure but says nothing about the visible name a reader sees. Alignment requires that visible identity to match the domain that passed the check.
questions.hint: Consider a name the attacker simply typed into the header.

questions.topic: Why forwarding breaks sender authorisation
questions.learningObjective: Determine which observation shows why forwarded mail loses sender authorisation.
questions.stem: Ticket MAIL-58 lists three observations about forwarded mail and asks which one explains why authorisation no longer holds.

options.text: The forwarded copy carries the original signature, so the original sender is still its author
options.misconception: assumes carrying the original signature keeps the author

options.text: The forwarded copy was composed by the forwarder, so the original sender is not its author
The forwarded copy left the organisation, so the receiving server can no longer read the headers
options.misconception: believes leaving the organisation strips the header information

options.text: The forwarded copy was scanned by a filter, so the original signature can no longer be verified
options.misconception: thinks any filtering step breaks signature verification

questions.explanation: Authorisation attaches to whoever composed the message the reader received. The forwarder composed that copy, so the original sender no longer stands behind it.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: The registration step signed resolution does not cover
questions.learningObjective: Explain why the registration step lies outside signed name resolution.
questions.stem: Ticket DNS-40 asks for a written explanation of why the registration step cannot be covered by the signed records used during resolution.

answer.exemplar: Registration decides which organisation is recorded as the holder of a name and which registrar may publish the delegation for it. Those facts live in registrar and registry systems, are negotiated commercially, and are not signed with the zone keys that the resolver checks, so the resolver has no cryptographic way to confirm them.

questions.explanation: Signed resolution proves only that the records came from a key descending from the trusted anchor. The registrar relationship is a commercial fact recorded elsewhere, outside what a resolver can verify.
questions.hint: Ask what a zone key can and cannot attest to.

stimulus.body: A trace excerpt in ticket NAT-27 shows one session from an internal host 10.0.4.19 to a remote service. The server replies to 198.51.100.24, and the reply is translated back to 10.0.4.19 before it reaches the host.

questions.stem: Given the trace described in ticket NAT-27, which detail of the session is still visible to the remote server?

options.text: The remote server sees the internal address 10.0.4.19 in the reply it sends back
options.misconception: believes the internal address survives translation inbound

options.text: The remote server sees a public address on the reply it sends back to the gateway
The remote server sees the port number the internal application originally chose
options.misconception: assumes the original transport port is preserved remotely

options.text: The remote server sees the internal address inside a header added by the gateway
options.misconception: thinks translation reveals the internal address in a header

questions.explanation: Translation rewrites the source address and usually the source port outbound, then reverses the mapping inbound. The server replies to the public address, so the internal address and original port stay hidden.

options.text: It diverts traffic for the announced prefix, and it gives the attacker the ability to read that traffic
options.misconception: believes route control also yields the ability to read traffic

options.text: It leaves traffic routing untouched, and it gives the attacker no ability to read that traffic
options.misconception: thinks an unauthorised announcement has no effect on forwarding

options.text: It diverts traffic for the announced prefix, and it gives the attacker no ability to read that traffic
It diverts traffic for the announced prefix, and it gives the attacker rights over the target
options.misconception: confuses diverted traffic with control of the target

questions.explanation: An unauthorised announcement changes the path traffic for that prefix takes, so the attacker receives or blocks it. It decrypts nothing, because announcements carry no keys and grant no device access.

options.misconception: thinks the record lists forwarding services and addresses

options.text: A list of the sending hosts and networks permitted to originate mail for that domain

options.misconception: believes the signature protects the delivery path

options.text: Changing one character of the body invalidates the signature even though the headers are untouched
Changing the sending date invalidates the signature even though the body is untouched

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: Why forwarding breaks sender authorisation
questions.learningObjective: Explain how forwarding changes the trust relationship for a received message.
questions.stem: Ticket MAIL-74 asks for a written explanation of why forwarding a signed message weakens the authorisation a receiver can rely on.

answer.exemplar: The signature was made over the original message by the original sender, and it still verifies on that text. A forwarder then creates a new message containing that text, so the receiver is dealing with something the original sender never composed or approved. The signature therefore attests to an inner message rather than to the message in hand, and the forwarding organisation has inserted itself into the trust path.

questions.explanation: The signature still proves the inner message came from its signer, but the copy in the reader hands was composed by the forwarder. The forwarding organisation has inserted itself between signer and reader.
questions.hint: Compare who composed the text with who signed it.

options.text: The answer was trusted because the newest key was already present in the resolver cache
options.misconception: believes the resolver held the zone newest signing key

options.text: The answer was trusted because the resolver accepted the chain without validating any key
options.misconception: assumes the chain was trusted without any validation

options.text: The answer was trusted because of the older chain, even though the zone has since adopted a newer key
The answer was trusted because the delegation chain bypassed the trust anchor entirely
options.misconception: thinks the accepted chain avoided the trust anchor altogether

questions.explanation: The resolver validates against keys it holds, so an older chain that still reaches the anchor stays acceptable after a rollover. Trust in the chain, not recency of the record, justified the answer.
questions.hint: Recency and valid chain are different tests.

questions.topic: What the alignment rule in a reporting record adds
questions.learningObjective: Identify the forgery that an alignment comparison defeats.

stimulus.body: An excerpt in ticket POL-22 gives the policy record for a sending domain and then adds a separate condition that the visible sender name and the visible domain must correspond under a relaxed comparison. The ticket asks which condition the relaxed comparison is meant to defeat.

questions.stem: In the policy described in ticket POL-22, which forgery does the relaxed comparison between names defeat?

options.text: A sender who makes the visible name look like the protected domain without using that infrastructure
A sender who obtains a valid signature from the domain and then alters the signed body text
options.misconception: believes the comparison detects tampering with body text

options.text: A sender who steals the domain signing key from the domain own mail administrator
options.misconception: thinks the name comparison detects a stolen signing key

options.text: A sender who forwards legitimate mail from inside the domain to an unrelated address

questions.learningObjective: Explain why signed resolution cannot reach the registration step.
questions.stem: Ticket DNS-78 asks for a written account of why the registration step is outside the reach of signed name resolution.

answer.exemplar: Signing protects the chain of records a resolver follows to answer a query, and each of those records is signed by a key that descends from a trusted anchor. The registration of a name with a registrar is a commercial act recorded in registry and registrar systems; no zone key signs it, no resolver can check it, and a resolver that trusted it would have to believe a registrar rather than verify anything.

questions.explanation: Signed resolution verifies keys and record relationships a resolver can check directly. Registration is a commercial fact held elsewhere, so no cryptographic mechanism available to a resolver reaches it.

options.misconception: thinks an exhausted address pool removes the need for translation

options.misconception: assumes the capture point sits outside the translating gateway

questions.explanation: Translation happens at the gateway, so anything running inside the network sees the original internal addresses. A capture taken outside sees only the public address, which is why the two views disagree.

answer.exemplar: Before forwarding, the reader could treat the message as authored by the domain that signed it, under a policy that the receiver had checked. answer.exemplar: The signature is computed over the signed body and signed headers with the sender private key, and any change to that material makes the check fail, so it detects alteration and ties the content to a key holder. questions.topic: What an untrusted route announcement permits
questions.learningObjective: Explain what a route announcement gives its sender and what it withholds.
questions.stem: Ticket NET-71 asks for a written explanation of what a route announcement can and cannot give the party that sends it.

answer.exemplar: A route announcement is a request to send traffic for a prefix down a particular path, so by making one the sender can cause that traffic to reach equipment it controls, or to be withheld entirely. It carries no proof of identity, no cryptographic protection for the traffic, and no authority over the destination systems; accepting it is a separate and fallible decision made by each router along the way.

questions.explanation: The announcement is a request about forwarding, so it lets its originator attract or withhold traffic for a prefix. It conveys no proof of identity, no protection for the traffic, and no access to the destination.
questions.hint: Ask what an announcement is asking the network to do.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What a sender policy record states and who evaluates it
questions.learningObjective: Explain what running a policy check contributes to a receiver decision.

stimulus.body: A ticket quotes a policy record for a sending domain that permits mail only from a small number of known hosts, and it notes that the receiving organisation runs the check against every message from that domain. The ticket asks what the check contributes to the receiving organisation decision.

questions.stem: In ticket MSG-118, what does running the check contribute to the receiver decision?

options.text: It proves that the person who wrote the message works for the domain
options.misconception: believes the check confirms the human author works there

options.text: It guarantees that the message body has not been changed since it was written
options.misconception: thinks the check guarantees the body is unmodified

options.text: It removes the need to examine the visible sender name against the domain
options.misconception: assumes the check makes alignment unnecessary

options.text: It separates mail from the domain infrastructure from mail that merely claims to be from it

questions.explanation: The check compares sending infrastructure against an authorised list, separating genuine domain mail from mail that merely claims the domain. It does not identify a person or replace the identity check.
questions.hint: Ask what the check can tell that the visible name cannot.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What a domain-key signature deliberately excludes
questions.learningObjective: Separate what an observer learns from a domain-key signature from what they do not.
questions.stem: Ticket MAIL-121 asks for two facts about domain-key signatures: what an observer can learn from one, and what an observer cannot learn from it.

options.text: That the content came from the key holder, and not what the content says or who the person was
That the content came from the key holder, and what the content says because the key signs the words
options.misconception: believes the signature reveals the meaning of the text

options.text: That the content stayed secret from intermediaries, and not who the person behind it was
options.misconception: assumes signing makes the content unreadable in transit

options.text: That the content came from the key holder, and whether the recipient actually received it
options.misconception: believes a signature confirms delivery to the recipient

questions.explanation: The signature establishes that the key holder produced the content and that it was not altered. It exposes nothing about the meaning of the text, the person behind the key, or the delivery outcome.
questions.hint: Ask what the signature reveals about origin rather than content.
